The contents of this course integrate interdisciplinary knowledge from physics, chemistry and life sciences. # Course Content

| | Topics | **Highlights of Fundamental Concepts** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Basic concepts in thermodynamics and physical chemistry | Free energy, entropy, chemical potential, osmotic pressure, chemical equilibrium, solution thermodynamics (Doi Chapter 1,2) |
| 2. | Molecular interactions | van der Waals interaction; electrostatics of biomolecules; electrostatic interaction between colloids and molecules; depletion force (Doi Chapter 2; Jones Chapter 2) |
| 3. | Molecules in motion | Diffusion; reaction kinetics; enzymatic reactions; molecular switching and allosteric regulation; coupling between chemical reactions and diffusion process (Nelson Chapters 3,4; Doi Chapter 6) |
| 4. | Materials in motion | Basic concepts in continuum mechanics/biomechanics and rheology, viscosity, viscoelastic behavior of fluids, low Reynolds hydrodynamics (Doi Chapter 3,9; Phillips Chapters 10, 11; Jones Chapter 5; Nelson Chapter 5) |
| 5. | Interfacial phenomena | Surface tension, Laplace pressure, capillarity, wetting. (Doi Chapter 4; Jones Chapter 9) |
| 6. | Diffusion in living processes | Fundamental limit on cell size; Nernst potential across membranes; chemical signaling of bacteria and general gradient sensing (Nelson Chapters 4,11; Phillips Chapter 13,14) |
| 7. | Self-assembly of biomolecules and molecular machines | Molecular self-assembly driven by entropic force; Molecular motors that couple diffusion, free energy transduction and enzymatic reactions (Nelson Chapters 8,9,10; Phillips Chapter 14) |
| 8. | Energetics and electrical behavior of cells | Energy metabolism and chemiosmosis; ion channels and action potentials; nerve impulse (Nelson Chapters 11,12) |
| 9. | Dynamics in the cell | Dynamics of gene and protein regulatory networks; robustness and adaptation of regulatory networks; genetic oscillator (Phillips Chapter 19) |
| 10. | Mechanics and motile behavior of cells | Mechanical response of cells; mechanisms of self-propulsion in bacterial and eukaryotic cells (Phillips Chapters 10,11,12; Nelson Chapter 5) |

# Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

| 1. | manage to derive and compute mechanical and statistical variables that characterize soft and living matter systems, such as elastic modulus, viscosity, diffusivity, chemical potential, and osmotic pressure. |
| --- | --- |
| 2. | explain the physical mechanisms underlying various essential living processes, such as biomolecular self-assembly, biological information processing, cellular physiology, and cell motility. |
| 3. | describe and explain general biological phenomena in terms of physical concepts. |

courses.title: Optical Observational Astronomy
courses.description: The course aims to provide students an introduction to the principles and techniques of observational astronomy in the optical waveband, including the principles of the telescopes and instruments, and hands-on experience of data acquisition and data analysis. The topics covered will include the motivation of observations, targets to observe, practical challenges of observations, the telescopes, instruments, detectors, imaging and spectroscopic methods, data calibration, processing, and analysis methods. PHYS3430 and PHYS3440 are independent courses from each other.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: PHYS2401 and PHYS2711, or their equivalents, or permission of instructor.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. List different types of targets of astronomical observations, their radiation mechanisms, and how they can be observed.
2. Describe the practical challenges of optical observations posed by the properties of light, the atmosphere, the interstellar medium, and the limitations of current technologies, etc.
3. Explain the working principles of different types of telescopes, instruments, and detectors.
4. Collect, calibrate, and analyze data taken through astronomical observations.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Motivation and targets of observations
Motivation, astronomical objects to observe, and their radiation mechanisms.

2. Practical challenges of optical observations
The moving sky, effects of the atmosphere, natural and artificial light pollution, limits of observations.

3. Optical telescopes and instrumentations
Types of telescopes and mounts, angular resolution, plate scale, optical aberrations, imaging and spectroscopy instrumentations.

4. CCD/CMOS Detectors and calibration
CCD, CMOS, bias, read noise, dark current, gain, flat fielding, method to measure these properties.

5. Photometry
Magnitude system, filters, background subtraction, aperture photometry, curve of growth, SNR equation, PSF photometry, and calibration.

* 6.* Spectroscopy
Slit spectroscopy, fiber spectroscopy, integral field spectroscopy, spectral extraction, wavelength and flux calibration.

7. Hands-on data acquisition and analysis
Conducted in parallel with topics 4-6, practice the methods on data collection, processing, and analysis.
courses.required_readings:
1. Observational Astronomy, 2nd Edition, by D. Scott Birney, Guillermo Gonzalez, & David Oesper. (Online access through CUHK library)
2. Handbook of CCD Astronomy, 2nd Edition, by Steve B. Howell. (Online access through CUHK library)

# Course Description

Topics include: growth and fabrication of nano-size materials, applying quantum physics to semiconducting heterostructures and quantum dots, band theory and its application to photonic and plasmonic crystals, physics and applications of nano-photonics and plasmonics, and applications of perturbation theories to nano-electronics and nano-photonics. # Course Content

| | Topics | **Highlights of Fundamental Concepts** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Growth and fabrication of nano-size materials | Foundations of thin film growth techniques, clean room technologies and photolithography. |
| 2. | Applications of quantum physics in different potentials and its applications in semiconducting heterostructures and quantum dots | Review on basic concepts of quantum physics and results of different potential wells. Applications of quantum physics in resonant tunneling junction, two-dimensional electron gas, split gate technology, artificial atom, single electron transistor, etc. |
| 3. | Essential band theory of solids | Periodic potential and Bloch formalism |
| 4. | Nano-photonics and plasmonics | Review on basic electromagnetism. Basic concepts of plasmonics. Application of Bloch formalism to photonic and plasmonic crystals. Applications of nano-photonics and plasmonics. |

| 5. | describe and explain the band theory of solids, in particular the Bloch formalism |
| 6. | describe and explain the basics of nano-photonics and plasmonics |
| 7. | apply Bloch formalism to photonic and plasmonic crystals |
| 8. | apply first and second order time-independent perturbation theories to solve perturbed potential wells, degeneracy problem, etc. |
| 9. | apply time-dependent perturbation theory to electronic transitions, optical properties of solids, nano-electronics and nano-photonics |

courses.description: This course provides an overview of the basic principles and applications of various branches of modern optics physics. Topics covered include: geometrical optics, waves optics, polarization, Fourier optics, introduction to laser physics and nonlinear optics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: PHYS3041 or its equivalents, or permission of instructor.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Demonstrate knowledge about optical elements/devices and how to use them to build basic optical systems
2. Describe and explainthe wave nature of light through the propagation of light, light matter interactions, interference and diffraction
3. Demonstrate the understanding of lasers and interpret the meaning of coherence of light
4. Demonstrate knowledge of modern developments of optical physics and optical technologies
5. Appreciate important applications of optical physics
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Electromagnetic waves
Wave equations. Harmonic waves. Plane, cylindrical and spherical waves. Superposition of waves. Standing waves. Phase and group velocities. The propagation of light, Huygen’s and Fermat principles, reflection, refraction, light matter interaction

2. Geometrical optics
Lenses, mirrors, prisms, fiber optics, aberrations, introduction to ray tracing, optical systems

3. Polarization
Nature of polarization, birefringence, polarizers and retarders, applications of polarization

4. Interference
Examples of two-beam interference. Stokes relations. Multiple-beam interference. Theories and applications of optical interferometers. Resonators.

5. Diffraction
General concepts of diffraction. Examples of Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction. Diffraction grating and its applications.

6. Modern optics (Optional)
Coherence and Fourier optics, lasers, holography, introduction of nonlinear optics

7. Advanced topics (Optional)
Super-resolution optical microscopy, optical trapping, metamaterials

courses.title: Photonics: Materials and Devices
courses.description: A broad survey of the materials used and the generation, transmission, modulation, detection and harvesting of light by various optoelectronic devices. Emphases are placed on the operational principles and applications of both devices and materials in communications, data processing, light emission, lasing, light control, photovoltaics and photodetection, as well as on related state-of-the-art scientific research.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Instrumentation II
courses.description: Principles, instrumentation, experiments and data interpretation of spectroscopy, thermal analysis, microscopy and other instrumentation. Laboratory experiments for practice and illustration of the subject matter.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To gain a general understanding of the development of modern instrumentations and know their significance to the society.
2. To make connections of the concepts acquired in other physics courses (e.g. thermal physics, quantum physics and solid state physics) to practical experiments.
3. To realize that one should know the working principles in order to gain deep understandings when performing research with these modern instruments.
4. To learn some commonly used experimental techniques and facilities in physics research, and have the knowledge of other instrumentations not discussed in details at the class.
5. To gain hands-on experience with available modern instruments in the department by carrying out some experiments, such as thermal analysis, atomic force microscopy, and optical microscopy.
6. To acquire experimental skills related to their research for further studies.
courses.course_syllabus:
Transducers and sensors: (~ 5 lectures)
Types of transducers and sensors. Figures of merit of transducers and sensors: Accuracy, repeatability, resolution, sensitivity, dynamic range.

Signal conditioning, propagation and conversion: (~ 4 lectures)
Amplification: gain, bandwidth, gain bandwidth product, impedance matching.
Analog-digital conversion and sampling: analog to digital, digital to analog, Nyquist theorem aliasing. Transmission media: types, bandwidth and noise restrictions.

Noise: (~ 4 lectures)
Sources of fundamental noise, thermal noise, shot noise, 1/f noise, signal to noise ratio, noise equivalent power and detectability. Environmental noise: sources and minimization, electrical pickup, electromagnetic interference and radio frequency interference, power-line-coupled noise, ground loops, shielding, grounding.

Signal Transmission: (~ 3 lectures)
Filtering and discriminating, averaging. Phase sensitive detection, multichannel averager, gated integrator.

Vacuum techniques: (~ 4 lectures)
Pumps: rotary, diffusion, turbomolecular, ion, cryo. Seals, flanges, feedthroughs, and valves.
Pressure gauges: thermoconductive, ion, Penning. Gas flow: controllers, flowmeters. Leak detection.

Instrumentation for Integrated-circuit fabrication: (~2 lectures)
Epitaxial growth, masking, etching, plasma etching.

Medical Instrumentation: (~2 lectures)
EEG, ECG, EMG, magnetic resonance imaging, tomography.

courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the basic concepts and theoretical techniques of the quantum theory of many-body systems at zero-temperature as well as at finite temperature. Topics covered include: second quantization, Green's functions at zero-temperature, Green's functions at finite temperature, perturbation theory and Feynman diagram, equations of motion of the Green's functions, linear response theory, and applications of many-body theory in condensed matter physics.

Topics include symmetries groups and conservation laws, relativistic quantum mechanics, perturbation theory, quantum electrodynamics, quantum chromodynamics, weak interactions, the Standard Model, gauge symmetry, spontaneous symmetry breaking, Higgs mechanism, neutrino oscillations.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in Theoretical Physics (Advanced Computational Physics)
courses.description: This course is intended to provide a solid training in the advanced techniques of contemporary computational physics. Topics covered include: classical Monte Carlo method and applications, algorithms in matrix operations and ODE PDE solvers, many-body system optimizations, A brief introduction to Density Functional Theory, random systems, and selected topics of current interest in computational physics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To appreciate the connection between computation methods and physics research.
2. To realize that one should perform detailed calculations in order to gain deep understandings of underline physics for many fascinating observations.
3. To learn some commonly used computational techniques in physics research, and have the knowledge of other computational techniques not discussed in details at the class.
4. To carry out calculations of some basic quantities (such as ground state energy, magnetization and magnetic susceptibility, single-particle density) describing properties of typical physical systems.
5. To make connections to concepts acquired in other physics courses, e.g., thermal physics, quantum physics, mathematical physics, solid state physics, and statistical physics.
6. To perform calculations involving diagonalizing Hamiltonian matrix with the Fermi-Dirac statistics, and to relate results to manybody physical problems both non-interacting and interacting particles.
7. To perform non-perturbative calculations by using the advanced computational techniques, such Monte Carlo integration for classical systems.
8. To acquire mathematical skills related to integration and data analysis.
9. To acquire and appreciate the use of random number in physics research. To be able to write computer program to generate random numbers and
perform simulations.
10. To acquire the basic principles for further studies on computer simulation of many-body systems.

3. Solving ODE and PDE
4. Monte Carlo Simulations
5. Density functional theory
6. Other topics, such as machine learning. Parallel computing.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Modern Atomic Physics
courses.description: This course will discuss various fundamental topics of modern atomic physics at the postgraduate level. The first part of the course focuses on atomic structures, the semi-classical theory of atom-light interactions and their application to the understanding of laser cooling and related topics. The second part is on atom-atom interactions at ultracold temperatures, including its application to evaporative cooling for reaching quantum degeneracy. An advanced topics section is also included to introduce the most recent developments in this field. Students should have undergraduate level Quantum Mechanics before taking this course.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For MSc Physics
For MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
For MPhil-PhD Physics
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To apply the fundamental knowledge of quantum mechanics to understand atomic structures.
2. To understand interactions between light-atom, and atom-atom and to solve common real-world problems.
3. To understand the physical basis of the recent development in ultracold AMO physics.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Review of quantum mechanics: Schrödinger’s equation, probability density, operator and Hamiltonian, observables, uncertainty principle, angular momentum, spin.
2. Atomic structure: Hydrogen atom, fine structure, hyperfine structure, alkali atoms, Zeeman Effect, Stark Effect.
3. Atom-light interaction: Einstein coefficients, driven two-level systems, Rabi frequency, density matrix and optical Bloch equations, relaxation, saturation and lineshape, Doppler-free laser spectroscopy.
4. Laser cooling and trapping: Scattering force, slowing of atomic beams, optical molasses, cooling limits, magneto-optical trap, optical dipole trap.
5. Ultracold collisions, evaporative cooling: Introduction to scattering theory, partial wave expansion, scattering length, elastic scattering, inelastic collisions, evaporative cooling.
6. Bose Einsten condensation of dilute atomic gases: Critical temperature, condensate fraction, macroscopic wave function, Gross-Pitaevskii equation, Thomas-Fermi approximation.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Introduction to Biophysics
courses.description: Biophysics investigates biological phenomena using theoretical and experimental approaches derived from physics, such as statistical mechanics, fluid mechanics, and optics. This course provides an introduction to biophysics for postgraduate students with no biology background. Students will be introduced to basic biology and physics concepts relevant to the course, followed by topics including the functions of biomolecules, dynamics of regulatory networks, physics of cellular behavior, and recent development of frontier biophysics techniques. Through this course, students will become familiar with the scope and basic approaches of biophysics research, learn how to perform computer simulations on biomolecules, and develop interest in exploring new territories of biophysics. Students should have undergraduate level thermodynamics and statistical mechanics before taking this course.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Physics, MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg or MPhil-PhD Physics
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) To understand basic concepts in biophysics.
(2) To develop knowledge of commonly-used methods in computational and experimental biophysics research.
(3) To develop interest in applying physics concepts and tools to study living systems.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction to biology: Proteins and other biomolecules inside cells; Central dogma of molecular biology; Types of cells.
2. Basic concepts in biophysics: Friction and diffusion; Energy, entropy, Brownian motors; Water as the solvent for life; Viscosity and low-Reynolds number world.
3. Molecules, machines and mechanisms; Enzymes and molecular machines; Membranes and machines in membranes; Bioelectricity and nerve impulses.
4. Techniques in biophysics research: Computer modeling and simulation; Molecular dynamics simulations; Commonly used programs and force fields; analysis of simulation results. A brief survey of single-molecule techniques.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in Experimental Physics (Thin Film Physics and Technology)
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the physical properties of thin films as well as the preparation methods. Topics covered include: vacuum science and technology, thin film deposition techniques, growth processes and modes, characterization, epitaxy, lattice engineering, optical and electrical properties of thin films. State-of-the-art scientific research on thin film preparation and properties will also be selectively introduced.

courses.learning_outcomes:

(2) To understand the basic principles of vacuum science and technology that are related to thin-film deposition techniques.
(3) To understand the thermodynamics of evaporation and learn the basic principles of evaporation.
(4) To acquire the basic knowledge about adsorption, surface diffusion, nucleation, and structure development that are involved in thin-film deposition.
(5) To acquire the basic knowledge of epitaxial deposition.
(6) To learn the basic knowledge of chemical vapor deposition.
(7) To learn the basic techniques of measuring the physical and chemical properties of thin films.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Semiconductor Physics and Devices
courses.description: This course discusses the physics of semiconductors and the principles behind selected applications. The physics of the electronic band structures, electrons and holes dynamics, effects of impurities, semiconductor statistics, and lattice vibrations will be discussed, using the technologically important semiconductors such as Si, Ge, and GaAs as examples. Transport properties and optical properties of semiconductors will then be treated. The principles of some common devices based on semiconductors will be introduced. The physics of selected semiconductor heterostructures will also be discussed. Using semiconductors as the context, the students will learn and appreciate how quantum physics, statistical physics, and elementary solid state physics can be applied to understand much of semiconducting materials, which have transformed and will continue to transform technologies and the world.

Topics to be discussed include:

Principles of p-n junctions and related devices
Semiconductor lasers and photodevices
Heterostructures, superlattices and nanostructures
Applications of heterostructures
Metal-semiconductor devices
